summary:
What did you develop?
We made an interactive 3D multi- and single-player space mission design game that includes a walkable 52 meters two-deck ark, salvable cargo crates, physical components installation, repair stations, and cinematic rocket launches.

How does it address the challenge?
Our game platform includes two different game modes—Research Expedition Mode (which concentrates on collecting data about Earth, Moon, Mars, LEO, MEO orbits) and Escape Earth Mode (dealing with interstellar colonization and old stuff stories), thus combining aerospace engineering challenges with gaming mechanics.

Why is it important?
The platform helps to translate the science of orbital mechanics, budgeting, and propulsion physics into an entertaining and educational experience for the players who learn what makes missions successful or not.
details:
What it does and how it works:

  • Core Gameplay: An interactive 3D space mission design and survival simulator where single players or teams of up to four collaborate to design, build, salvage, and launch missions from a dying Earth.
  • Walkable 3D Environment: Features a massive 52-meter, two-deck ark interior complete with boarding ramps, wall-mounted ladders (press E to climb), hull collision blocking, and interactive salvage crates that players can explore and manage.

Two Distinct Modes:

  • Research Expedition Mode: Focuses on scientific data collection across Earth, Moon, Mars, LEO, and MEO orbits with guided explanations and no countdown timer.
  • Escape Earth Mode: Opens with an abandoned-Earth cinematic briefing with synthetic radio narration, allowing players to escape a dying Earth for five interstellar destinations (Proxima Centauri b, TRAPPIST-1e, LHS 1140 b, Kepler-186f, and Kepler-452b) using four advanced interstellar propulsion systems (Laser-Beamed Sail, Nuclear Pulse/Fusion Drive, Antimatter-Catalyzed Drive, and Bussard Ramjet).
  • Interactive Engineering & Repair Loops: Features live top-left counters for Mass (kg) and Budget Credits, hover component inspection, and Among Us-style interactive repair tasks where damaged rocket parts glow red and require direct player fixing before launch.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

  • Educational Engagement: Translates complex aerospace engineering, orbital mechanics, and propulsion physics into accessible, gamified mechanics.
  • Experiential Learning: Teaches players why real-world space missions succeed or fail through live resource feedback, budget management, and post-mission flight evaluation reports.
  • Collaborative Problem-Solving: Fosters teamwork by allowing up to four players to share design controls, balance critical constraints, and divide responsibilities.

Tools, Technologies, and Software: Developed as a browser-based 3D simulation utilizing interactive web UI, 3D rendering engines, audio/touch compatibility, and Nilo AI platform infrastructure.Grounded in authentic scientific and aerospace reference frameworks, including NASA Exoplanet Archive parameters, NASA SLS/Artemis reference specs, and NASA Innovative Advanced Concepts (NIAC) breakthrough propulsion studies.


Project Creativity: Blends survival-crafting elements (salvaging large crates in a walkable multi-deck starship, physical component placement, and task-based emergency repairs) with rigorous astrophysical data.Offers a unique narrative contrast between near-term scientific exploration (Research mode) and desperate interstellar colonization (Escape Earth mode).

Factors Considered by the Team:

  • Real-World Engineering Constraints: Balanced strict physical limits including total spacecraft mass, available power, budget credits, communications capacity, data rates, and mission lifetime.
  • Accessibility vs. Complexity: Designed guided explanations and recommended starter configurations for beginners while keeping advanced engineering choices (such as antimatter magnetic containment safety and battery sizing) active for experienced players.
  • Consequence-Driven Design: Ensured that every design decision carries meaningful trade-offs (e.g., adding scientific instruments increases mass, power consumption, cost, and data generation; undersized batteries cause launch failures).

TRAPPIST-1e	 40.7 light-years	 0.92 Earth radii; 0.69 Earth masses	 Ultra-cool Red Dwarf (7-planet system)	 Multi-World Choice: Low gravity eases landing fuel costs, and neighboring planets allow backup colonization if one fails.  LHS 1140 b	48.8 light-years	~1.73 Earth radii; ~5.6 Earth masses	Quiet Red Dwarf; likely ocean/ice world	High-Gravity Landing: Dense atmosphere aids aerobraking, but higher gravity demands powerful retro-rockets for touchdown.  Kepler-186f	582 light-years	~1.17 Earth radii	Cooler K/M-dwarf; outer habitable zone	Deep-Time Generation Ship: Demands maximum cryosleep reliability and closed-loop recycling for multi-century transit.  Kepler-452b	1,800 light-years	~1.63 Earth radii	G2-type star (closest Sun twin)	Endgame "New Earth": Ideal solar spectrum for Earth crops without UV flare risk, but requires maximum fusion/antimatter delta-v.

Launch & Cislunar Constraints (Research Expedition Mode): Payload limits, liftoff thrust, and mission endurance baselines were adapted from official NASA Space Launch System (SLS) and Orion / Artemis Program reference specifications.

Theoretical Propulsion Concepts (Mission: Escape Earth Mode): Interstellar propulsion classes—including directed-energy laser sails, nuclear fusion, and antimatter-catalyzed concepts—were adapted from research funded by NASA Innovative Advanced Concepts (NIAC) and NASA Glenn Research Center breakthrough propulsion studies. (Note: Specific game balance figures such as build credits, simplified fuel masses, and gameplay trade-off multipliers were designed by our team for simulation gameplay.)
